# Go-to-Market Plan: Building DTC Without Losing the Base

## 1. The Strategic Frame

The failed pilot failed for a reason worth naming: it was designed as a *store*, and it was *discovered*. Both are fatal. A supplier web store that sells the same items at competitive prices is, from a buyer's perspective, a competitor with better margins and no shelf rent. Discovery converts an economic disagreement into a trust breach, which is much harder to repair.

The reframe that makes this survivable: **DTC is not a sales channel first — it is a demand-generation, data, and innovation asset whose commercial output happens to be revenue.** Everything in this plan flows from a single test applied to every decision:

> *Does this make the retailer's business with us better, worse, or neutral — and can we prove it with numbers they trust?*

The deal on offer to retailers is explicit and repeated in every conversation:

**Three commitments and one ask.**
- **Commitment 1 — Price:** we will never be the cheapest place to buy a comparable item. Ever. Publicly, verifiably.
- **Commitment 2 — Assortment:** the core, high-velocity SKUs your shoppers want will never be direct-exclusive. New items get a retail exclusivity window *before* they go broad.
- **Commitment 3 — Investment:** we will spend direct-channel learnings and a defined share of direct-channel gross profit *back into your business* — retail media, shopper marketing, validated new items, traffic driven to your stores.
- **The ask:** collaborative data access (clean room, loyalty insights) and credit for the demand we create.

Realistic three-year target: **8–12% of revenue direct**, and **30–40% of category buyers identified in a first-party database** — the second number matters more, and it does not come mainly from direct sales.

---

## 2. Channel Architecture

Five distinct roles, each with a defined job, assortment, and price position. The architecture is what prevents conflict; policy alone won't.

| Channel | Primary job | Assortment | Price position |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Brand Home (owned site)** | Brand education, product discovery, data capture, "where to buy" | Full catalog *visible*, partial catalog *buyable* | MSRP, never below |
| **Direct Commerce (within Brand Home)** | Subscription, personalization, systems, long tail | DTC-differentiated set only (§3) | MSRP or premium; value via service |
| **National retail (incl. the two majors)** | Volume, penetration, trial, physical availability | Core heroes, retailer-exclusive packs, seasonal | Retailer's discretion |
| **Retailer .com / marketplaces (1P & 3P)** | Digital shelf, search capture, review volume | Core + retailer-specific packs | Retailer's discretion; we support content/media |
| **Selective new physical** (specialty, club, international, B2B/gift) | Diversify concentration | Channel-appropriate packs | Channel norm |

**Two structural design choices that do the heavy lifting:**

**(a) "Where to Buy" is a first-class feature, not a footer link.** Every product page carries live retailer inventory and price via a syndication provider (Bazaarvoice/Channel Advisor/Swiftly-type widget), with the two majors positioned first. You then *report the click-throughs and attributed retail sales to each partner monthly*. This flips the narrative: your site becomes measurable top-of-funnel for them. Many suppliers find this widget drives more retail revenue than the direct cart does in year one — and it's the single most persuasive artifact you will ever bring to a buyer meeting.

**(b) Buyable ≠ visible.** The catalog is fully browsable for SEO, education, and reviews. Only the differentiated set is in the cart. This lets you own the search results without owning the transaction.

---

## 3. Product Differentiation: The Exclusivity Ladder

Direct assortment is defined by what retailers structurally *cannot* or *will not* profitably carry. This is a design constraint, not a concession.

**Tier A — Direct-only, structurally non-competitive**
- **Subscription/auto-replenishment** at commitment-based pricing (the discount is consideration for a 6–12 month commitment and logistics efficiency, not a naked price cut — an important distinction both commercially and legally).
- **Personalization and customization:** monogramming, engraving, custom scent/shade/formulation, made-to-order configurations. Zero shelf substitutability.
- **Complete systems and "whole-solution" bundles:** the razor + 4 blade types + case + stand, cross-category regimens, gifting sets.
- **Annual-supply / bulk packs** at pack sizes retailers don't stock.
- **Long tail:** discontinued-but-loved SKUs, replacement parts, consumables, accessories, size/shade extremes, refill-only formats.
- **Limited editions, collabs, community drops** at low volume — these are *marketing*, not revenue.
- **Certified refurb / cosmetically imperfect** inventory (also solves returns economics).

**Tier B — Retail-first innovation pipeline (the goodwill engine)**
- New items launch direct for a **90-day validation window**, then move to a **90–180 day exclusive window with the retailer who commits first**, then broad distribution.
- Direct becomes your test lab: you arrive at the line review with real conversion rates, repeat rates, review scores, and consumer verbatims instead of a concept board. Buyers reward this heavily — it de-risks *their* decision. Formalize it as a named program ("First Look") and give the two majors right of first refusal.

**Tier C — Shared core**
- Hero SKUs, identical spec, identical MSRP, direct-channel *never* promoted below the market. These exist so you are not accused of hiding behind technicalities. Their direct margin is irrelevant; their diplomatic value is high.

**Tier D — Retail-exclusive (the reciprocal gift)**
- Retailer-exclusive pack counts, value bundles, seasonal PDQ/displays, and one meaningful retailer-exclusive variant per major partner per year. **Exclusivity must run in both directions or the partnership story is hollow.**

**Pack-price architecture:** deliberately make cross-channel comparison apples-to-oranges. Retail carries 12ct and 24ct; direct carries 3-month (36ct) and annual (144ct) subscription formats. Different UPCs, different pack economics, no shelf-price screenshot that embarrasses anyone.

---

## 4. Pricing and Promotion Discipline

**The rule:** *We are the price ceiling, not the price floor.*

1. **Published unilateral MAP/IMAP policy** covering all channels **including our own**, with the direct channel explicitly bound. Publish it. Enforce it against grey-market sellers visibly — buyers care enormously about unauthorized sellers eroding their price integrity, and vigorous enforcement is a genuine gift you can deliver in month one.
2. **Value delivered through non-price levers,** which are unmatchable and non-comparable: free shipping thresholds, loyalty points, extended warranty/guarantee, free samples of adjacent products, early access, community, expert consultation, hassle-free returns, refill credits.
3. **Promotional blackout calendar.** No direct-channel promotion during each major partner's tentpole events (their branded sale weeks, holiday doorbusters, back-to-school). Where possible, *amplify* their events: your site's homepage promotes "Save at [Retailer] this week."
4. **No conquesting of retailer traffic.** Explicit paid-media exclusions: no bidding on `[retailer] + [our brand]` search terms, no retargeting of shoppers off retailer-owned properties, no geofenced in-store interception. Write this into the media brief and audit quarterly. This is the single most common trigger of buyer rage and the easiest to avoid.
5. **Shipping economics honesty.** Set the free-shipping threshold above single-unit purchase so direct buying skews to baskets and subscriptions rather than one-item price shopping. This is also how the direct P&L actually works.
6. **Trade investment held harmless.** Direct-channel growth does not become a pretext to cut trade spend. Freeze trade rates for 24 months at minimum and say so out loud — buyers will assume the opposite unless told.

**Illustrative economics** (to set internal expectations): a shared-core hero SKU at $24.99 MSRP might yield ~$11 wholesale revenue and ~$5.50 gross profit at retail; direct might yield $24.99 revenue and ~$13 gross profit *before* $6–9 of CAC, fulfillment, payments, and returns — netting $4–7 on a first order, and only becoming attractive on repeat. **Direct margin superiority is real but arrives on the second and third order, not the first.** Plan and communicate accordingly; a plan that promises immediate margin accretion will fail and will tempt the team into discounting.

---

## 5. Data Strategy

The critical insight: **direct transactions will never generate enough data volume to matter. Identity capture must be decoupled from direct purchase.**

**Layer 1 — Identity capture at retail scale (the real prize)**
- **Connected packaging:** QR codes on every unit across all channels, driving to product-specific registration/how-to-use/reorder pages. Target 3–8% scan rates rising over time; at your volumes this dwarfs direct order counts.
- **Warranty/product registration** with a genuine incentive (extended warranty, free accessory, refill credit).
- **Value-exchange content:** diagnostic quizzes, sizing/shade finders, meal or routine planners, how-to and troubleshooting — gated by email with progressive profiling rather than a wall.
- **Sampling and community programs**, ratings-and-reviews recruitment, customer service and warranty interactions, in-store QR on displays (co-branded, with retailer consent).
- **Receipt-based programs** and rebate mechanics for retail purchases where category economics allow.

**Layer 2 — Infrastructure**
- CDP as the identity spine with a consent management platform, documented lawful basis, preference center, and retention policy. Privacy compliance is not optional and a breach here would hand a partner a reason to walk.
- Consented first-party data feeding a clean-room-ready audience layer.
- Zero-party data (stated preferences, needs, household composition) prioritized over inferred — it's more accurate, more durable as third-party signal decays, and more defensible.

**Layer 3 — Give-to-get with retailers (this is what buys peace)**
- **Clean-room collaborations** (LiveRamp/Habu, plus retailer-native environments: Walmart Luminate/DSP, Roundel, 84.51°, Amazon Marketing Cloud). Match your first-party audiences to their loyalty data, measure incrementality, plan joint media. Retailers increasingly *want* this; suppliers who bring audiences get better outcomes.
- **A quarterly Insight Exchange:** you deliver a written pack to each major partner — category trend signals, emerging need states, new-item validation data, direct-channel search demand by DRIVE/geography, verbatims on their private-label competitive set where appropriate. Make it genuinely useful. Data you *share* is worth more than data you *hoard*, because sharing is what converts the direct channel from threat to asset in the buyer's mental model.
- **Reciprocal media commitment:** publicly commit a fixed percentage of direct-channel gross profit (start at 25–30%) to that partner's retail media network. This turns your direct growth into their revenue growth — a mechanical alignment that survives personnel changes.
- **Attribution reporting:** monthly report of direct-site sessions, where-to-buy clicks, and modeled retail sales attributed to your owned media, by partner.

**Guardrails:** never use retailer-provided data to target their shoppers off-platform; contract it explicitly. Never let the direct team see loyalty-level partner data. Document the firewall so you can prove it under challenge.

---

### 6.1 Repair the existing breach first

The pilot was discovered, which means you currently have a credibility deficit, not a strategy problem. Before anything launches:

- Bring the **Channel Charter** (below) as a written document. Written commitments are what buyers can defend internally to *their* bosses — which is the real dynamic. The buyer who called angrily was protecting themselves from their own leadership. Give them ammunition.

- **Assortment rules:** what is direct-only and why (the four structural categories), what is always available at retail, the First Look retail exclusivity window.
- **Pricing rules:** MSRP floor commitment, no lowest-price position, blackout calendar, MAP enforcement commitment.
- **Media rules:** the search/retargeting exclusion list, the retail media reinvestment percentage.
- **Data commitments:** what you'll share, clean-room participation, quarterly Insight Exchange.
- **Trade investment:** held-harmless commitment and duration.
- **Reporting:** what you'll report, how often, in what format.
- **Escalation path:** named executive, 48-hour response SLA.

### 6.3 Sequencing and cadence

|---|---|
| **Pre-launch −90 days** | Internal alignment; legal review of all supply agreements (MFN clauses, exclusivity, most-favored-pricing, audit rights) — you must know your contractual constraints before promising anything |
| **−75 days** | Top-to-top with each major partner; present Charter; solicit input and *actually incorporate some of it* |
| **−60 days** | Second-tier partners and distributors briefed; consistent script |
| **−45 days** | Integrate into Joint Business Planning: direct channel becomes a standing JBP agenda line item with agreed metrics |
| **−30 days** | Agree the year-one retailer-exclusive items and First Look calendar with each major |
| **Launch** | No press release positioning it as a store. Announce as "Brand Home" — an education and services destination. Partners see the site before it goes live |
| **Ongoing** | Monthly attribution report; quarterly Insight Exchange; semi-annual top-to-top; annual Charter refresh |

### 6.4 Language discipline

Ban internally and externally: *"disintermediation," "cutting out the middleman," "owning the customer," "DTC-first," "channel shift," "bypass."* These leak into decks, decks leak to buyers.

Use: *Brand Home, brand experience, innovation validation, demand generation, omnichannel, category growth, data collaboration, First Look, where-to-buy.*

### 6.5 Escalation playbook (for the next angry call)

Pre-build this before launch:
- **Named single owner** per account (the account lead, not the DTC lead) takes every call. Direct-channel team never negotiates with buyers.
- **24-hour acknowledgment, 5-day resolution** commitment.
- **Standing evidence pack**, refreshed monthly: where-to-buy click volume for that partner, modeled attributed retail sales, retail media spend delivered, First Look items given to them, price-parity audit results, MAP enforcement actions taken on their behalf.

Knowing the menu prevents panic concessions that unravel the architecture.

## 1. Blocking defect

**The document is unfinished.** It terminates mid-sentence: *"Get counsel involved early on: resale price maintenance (structure MAP as"*. §6.6 is the section where the plan's most legally exposed mechanisms would have been tested. It cannot be shipped or reviewed by an executive team in this state. Everything below assumes that gap gets closed — and the content that was cut is not incidental, for the reason in §2.

## 2. Substantive errors and internal contradictions

**(a) The MAP policy contradicts itself, and the contradiction is legally material.** §4.1 specifies a *"published unilateral MAP/IMAP policy."* The legal protection of a unilateral (Colgate-style) policy depends precisely on its being announced, not negotiated. §6.2 then makes pricing rules a clause in a **signed** Channel Charter shared with each major partner, and §6.3 instructs the team to *"solicit input and actually incorporate some of it."* A pricing policy negotiated with, and modified at the request of, your two largest customers is no longer unilateral — it is an agreement. Worse, giving **both** majors the same written promise that you will never undercut them creates a textbook hub-and-spoke fact pattern, with a signed document as the evidence. The plan needs to separate cleanly: (i) a genuinely unilateral pricing policy, announced not negotiated, and (ii) a partner-facing charter that covers assortment, media, data and reporting but is silent on committing *to them* about price. The current design maximizes both legal risk and discoverability.

Relatedly, the "tiered concession menu" (§6.5) includes *"pull a specific direct SKU or promotion"* and *"category-level assortment restriction"* **at a retailer's demand**. Acceding to a powerful customer's request to withdraw competing offerings is exactly the conduct that turns commercial diplomacy into an actionable restraint. It may still be the right business call — but it must be routed through counsel as a documented decision, not sit in a pre-approved playbook that middle managers execute under pressure.

**(b) The "no comparable price" promise doesn't survive unit-price math.** §3's pack architecture claims different pack counts mean *"no shelf-price screenshot that embarrasses anyone."* Retail buying teams manage price per ounce/count as their primary metric and their price-intelligence tools normalize automatically. A 144ct annual subscription pack will almost certainly land below the 12ct shelf item on $/unit — that is the whole point of it. The plan needs an explicit, auditable guardrail (e.g., *direct $/unit ≥ retailer everyday $/unit on the closest comparable, with subscription discounts benchmarked to MSRP and capped at X%*), plus an honest pre-brief that retail promotions will periodically undercut direct — which is fine and should be framed as proof of the commitment, not hidden.

**(c) The volume target is inconsistent with the constraints imposed on it.** The plan deliberately removes price advantage, excludes hero SKUs from the cart, bans conquesting and retargeting, and blacks out promotions in the highest-converting weeks — then targets **8–12% of total company revenue direct within three years**. There is no build-up (traffic × conversion × AOV × repeat rate × cohort retention) supporting it. From a near-zero base with a niche assortment, 3–6% is the more defensible planning number, and the plan should say so; an inflated top-line target is precisely what will tempt the team into the discounting the architecture forbids. Similarly, *"30–40% of category buyers identified"* is asserted, but the stated mechanism (3–8% QR scan rates) doesn't obviously get there. Show the arithmetic or lower the number.

**(d) The retail media pledge is poorly specified.** "25–30% of direct-channel gross profit" is unimpressive when direct GP is tiny (year one: a rounding error to a partner spending nine figures on media), and becomes a self-imposed tax on reinvestment exactly when DTC needs capital. It is also hard for a partner to audit. Absolute committed spend floors negotiated inside the JBP would be more credible in both directions.

**(e) Where-to-Buy attribution is presented as more persuasive than it is.** *"Modeled retail sales attributed to your owned media"* is supplier-marked homework; sophisticated buyers discount it heavily and may resent it. The claim that the widget *"drives more retail revenue than the direct cart"* is asserted without support and is load-bearing in the argument. Fix: propose **jointly agreed measurement** — incrementality tests run inside the retailer's own clean room / measurement environment (Luminate, Roundel, AMC) so the numbers are theirs, not yours.

**(f) Marketplace terms of service are unaddressed.** Layer 1's connected-packaging strategy (QR on every unit, driving to registration/reorder) conflicts with Amazon's prohibitions on diverting customers off-platform and on inserts soliciting contact; retailer.com 1P agreements often contain similar terms. Executing this at scale without a carve-out plan risks a suspension event on the very channel the plan relies on for digital shelf.

## 3. Material gaps

**(g) No downside case. This is the largest omission.** The prompt's central fact is that these partners *"have punished suppliers"* and that 55% of revenue sits with two accounts. The plan contains no war-game: what happens if a partner refuses the Charter, demands subscription be killed as a condition of the next line review, quietly reduces facings, cuts promotional support, or accelerates private label? There is no quantified exposure model (revenue/EBITDA impact of a 20% facing loss at Partner A), no trigger points, no kill switch, no BATNA, and no sequencing decision about *which* major to approach first and how to prevent them comparing notes. "Selective new physical (specialty, club, international, B2B/gift)" is one table row where a concentration-reduction roadmap with targets and timing should be.

**(h) No operating model or incentive design.** Who owns the direct P&L? How is a conflict between the sales VP and the DTC GM arbitrated, and by whom, on what timeline? Critically: a field sales organization compensated on retail sell-in will actively undermine DTC, and a DTC team on revenue targets will push discounts. Comp and internal transfer-pricing/credit rules are the real enforcement mechanism for everything in §4, and they are absent.

**(i) No investment case.** No capex/opex envelope, tech stack cost, headcount plan, fulfillment/3PL and returns economics, break-even timing, or funding source. The illustrative SKU math in §4 is useful but is not a channel P&L. An executive team cannot approve this document as written.

**(j) No demand-generation plan.** Having banned conquesting, retargeting off retailer properties, price leadership, and Q4 promotion, the plan never explains how traffic arrives. Owned/earned/creator strategy, SEO architecture, CRM lifecycle, subscription acquisition funnel and CAC assumptions by cohort are all missing — yet CAC of $6–9 is quoted as if solved.

**(k) No scorecard or stage gates.** There is a cadence table but no KPI set with targets and thresholds, no board review rhythm, and — importantly — no *partner health* leading indicators (share of shelf, distribution points, JBP score, promo support levels) tracked alongside DTC growth so conflict is detected before the angry call, not after.

**(l) Fulfillment/service quality unaddressed.** A direct channel that ships slower than the retailer it sits beside erodes brand equity and gives the buyer an easy talking point.

5. Add investment case and channel P&L with break-even.

7. Add demand-generation plan and CAC build.
8. Add KPI scorecard including partner-health leading indicators.

# Go-to-Market Plan: Building DTC Without Losing the Base

## 1. The Strategic Frame

The failed pilot failed for a reason worth naming: it was designed as a *store*, and it was *discovered*. Both are fatal. A supplier web store that sells the same items at competitive prices is, from a buyer's perspective, a competitor with better margins and no shelf rent. Discovery converts an economic disagreement into a trust breach, which is much harder to repair.

The reframe that makes this survivable: **DTC is not a sales channel first — it is a demand-generation, data, and innovation asset whose commercial output happens to be revenue.** Everything in this plan flows from a single test applied to every decision:

> *Does this make the retailer's business with us better, worse, or neutral — and can we prove it with numbers they trust?*

The deal on offer to retailers is explicit and repeated in every conversation:

**Three commitments and one ask.**
- **Commitment 1 — Price:** we will never be the cheapest place to buy a comparable item. Ever. Publicly, verifiably.
- **Commitment 2 — Assortment:** the core, high-velocity SKUs your shoppers want will never be direct-exclusive. New items get a retail exclusivity window *before* they go broad.
- **Commitment 3 — Investment:** we will spend direct-channel learnings and a defined share of direct-channel gross profit *back into your business* — retail media, shopper marketing, validated new items, traffic driven to your stores.
- **The ask:** collaborative data access (clean room, loyalty insights) and credit for the demand we create.

Realistic three-year target: **8–12% of revenue direct**, and **30–40% of category buyers identified in a first-party database** — the second number matters more, and it does not come mainly from direct sales.

---

## 2. Channel Architecture

Five distinct roles, each with a defined job, assortment, and price position. The architecture is what prevents conflict; policy alone won't.

| Channel | Primary job | Assortment | Price position |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Brand Home (owned site)** | Brand education, product discovery, data capture, "where to buy" | Full catalog *visible*, partial catalog *buyable* | MSRP, never below |
| **Direct Commerce (within Brand Home)** | Subscription, personalization, systems, long tail | DTC-differentiated set only (§3) | MSRP or premium; value via service |
| **National retail (incl. the two majors)** | Volume, penetration, trial, physical availability | Core heroes, retailer-exclusive packs, seasonal | Retailer's discretion |
| **Retailer .com / marketplaces (1P & 3P)** | Digital shelf, search capture, review volume | Core + retailer-specific packs | Retailer's discretion; we support content/media |
| **Selective new physical** (specialty, club, international, B2B/gift) | Diversify concentration | Channel-appropriate packs | Channel norm |

**Two structural design choices that do the heavy lifting:**

**(a) "Where to Buy" is a first-class feature, not a footer link.** Every product page carries live retailer inventory and price via a syndication provider (Bazaarvoice/Channel Advisor/Swiftly-type widget), with the two majors positioned first. You then *report the click-throughs and attributed retail sales to each partner monthly*. This flips the narrative: your site becomes measurable top-of-funnel for them. Many suppliers find this widget drives more retail revenue than the direct cart does in year one — and it's the single most persuasive artifact you will ever bring to a buyer meeting.

**(b) Buyable ≠ visible.** The catalog is fully browsable for SEO, education, and reviews. Only the differentiated set is in the cart. This lets you own the search results without owning the transaction.

---

## 3. Product Differentiation: The Exclusivity Ladder

Direct assortment is defined by what retailers structurally *cannot* or *will not* profitably carry. This is a design constraint, not a concession.

**Tier A — Direct-only, structurally non-competitive**
- **Subscription/auto-replenishment** at commitment-based pricing (the discount is consideration for a 6–12 month commitment and logistics efficiency, not a naked price cut — an important distinction both commercially and legally).
- **Personalization and customization:** monogramming, engraving, custom scent/shade/formulation, made-to-order configurations. Zero shelf substitutability.
- **Complete systems and "whole-solution" bundles:** the razor + 4 blade types + case + stand, cross-category regimens, gifting sets.
- **Annual-supply / bulk packs** at pack sizes retailers don't stock.
- **Long tail:** discontinued-but-loved SKUs, replacement parts, consumables, accessories, size/shade extremes, refill-only formats.
- **Limited editions, collabs, community drops** at low volume — these are *marketing*, not revenue.
- **Certified refurb / cosmetically imperfect** inventory (also solves returns economics).

**Tier B — Retail-first innovation pipeline (the goodwill engine)**
- New items launch direct for a **90-day validation window**, then move to a **90–180 day exclusive window with the retailer who commits first**, then broad distribution.
- Direct becomes your test lab: you arrive at the line review with real conversion rates, repeat rates, review scores, and consumer verbatims instead of a concept board. Buyers reward this heavily — it de-risks *their* decision. Formalize it as a named program ("First Look") and give the two majors right of first refusal.

**Tier C — Shared core**
- Hero SKUs, identical spec, identical MSRP, direct-channel *never* promoted below the market. These exist so you are not accused of hiding behind technicalities. Their direct margin is irrelevant; their diplomatic value is high.

**Tier D — Retail-exclusive (the reciprocal gift)**
- Retailer-exclusive pack counts, value bundles, seasonal PDQ/displays, and one meaningful retailer-exclusive variant per major partner per year. **Exclusivity must run in both directions or the partnership story is hollow.**

**Pack-price architecture:** deliberately make cross-channel comparison apples-to-oranges. Retail carries 12ct and 24ct; direct carries 3-month (36ct) and annual (144ct) subscription formats. Different UPCs, different pack economics, no shelf-price screenshot that embarrasses anyone.

---

## 4. Pricing and Promotion Discipline

**The rule:** *We are the price ceiling, not the price floor.*

1. **Published unilateral MAP/IMAP policy** covering all channels **including our own**, with the direct channel explicitly bound. Publish it. Enforce it against grey-market sellers visibly — buyers care enormously about unauthorized sellers eroding their price integrity, and vigorous enforcement is a genuine gift you can deliver in month one.
2. **Value delivered through non-price levers,** which are unmatchable and non-comparable: free shipping thresholds, loyalty points, extended warranty/guarantee, free samples of adjacent products, early access, community, expert consultation, hassle-free returns, refill credits.
3. **Promotional blackout calendar.** No direct-channel promotion during each major partner's tentpole events (their branded sale weeks, holiday doorbusters, back-to-school). Where possible, *amplify* their events: your site's homepage promotes "Save at [Retailer] this week."
4. **No conquesting of retailer traffic.** Explicit paid-media exclusions: no bidding on `[retailer] + [our brand]` search terms, no retargeting of shoppers off retailer-owned properties, no geofenced in-store interception. Write this into the media brief and audit quarterly. This is the single most common trigger of buyer rage and the easiest to avoid.
5. **Shipping economics honesty.** Set the free-shipping threshold above single-unit purchase so direct buying skews to baskets and subscriptions rather than one-item price shopping. This is also how the direct P&L actually works.
6. **Trade investment held harmless.** Direct-channel growth does not become a pretext to cut trade spend. Freeze trade rates for 24 months at minimum and say so out loud — buyers will assume the opposite unless told.

**Illustrative economics** (to set internal expectations): a shared-core hero SKU at $24.99 MSRP might yield ~$11 wholesale revenue and ~$5.50 gross profit at retail; direct might yield $24.99 revenue and ~$13 gross profit *before* $6–9 of CAC, fulfillment, payments, and returns — netting $4–7 on a first order, and only becoming attractive on repeat. **Direct margin superiority is real but arrives on the second and third order, not the first.** Plan and communicate accordingly; a plan that promises immediate margin accretion will fail and will tempt the team into discounting.

---

## 5. Data Strategy

The critical insight: **direct transactions will never generate enough data volume to matter. Identity capture must be decoupled from direct purchase.**

**Layer 1 — Identity capture at retail scale (the real prize)**
- **Connected packaging:** QR codes on every unit across all channels, driving to product-specific registration/how-to-use/reorder pages. Target 3–8% scan rates rising over time; at your volumes this dwarfs direct order counts.
- **Warranty/product registration** with a genuine incentive (extended warranty, free accessory, refill credit).
- **Value-exchange content:** diagnostic quizzes, sizing/shade finders, meal or routine planners, how-to and troubleshooting — gated by email with progressive profiling rather than a wall.
- **Sampling and community programs**, ratings-and-reviews recruitment, customer service and warranty interactions, in-store QR on displays (co-branded, with retailer consent).
- **Receipt-based programs** and rebate mechanics for retail purchases where category economics allow.

**Layer 2 — Infrastructure**
- CDP as the identity spine with a consent management platform, documented lawful basis, preference center, and retention policy. Privacy compliance is not optional and a breach here would hand a partner a reason to walk.
- Consented first-party data feeding a clean-room-ready audience layer.
- Zero-party data (stated preferences, needs, household composition) prioritized over inferred — it's more accurate, more durable as third-party signal decays, and more defensible.

**Layer 3 — Give-to-get with retailers (this is what buys peace)**
- **Clean-room collaborations** (LiveRamp/Habu, plus retailer-native environments: Walmart Luminate/DSP, Roundel, 84.51°, Amazon Marketing Cloud). Match your first-party audiences to their loyalty data, measure incrementality, plan joint media. Retailers increasingly *want* this; suppliers who bring audiences get better outcomes.
- **A quarterly Insight Exchange:** you deliver a written pack to each major partner — category trend signals, emerging need states, new-item validation data, direct-channel search demand by DRIVE/geography, verbatims on their private-label competitive set where appropriate. Make it genuinely useful. Data you *share* is worth more than data you *hoard*, because sharing is what converts the direct channel from threat to asset in the buyer's mental model.
- **Reciprocal media commitment:** publicly commit a fixed percentage of direct-channel gross profit (start at 25–30%) to that partner's retail media network. This turns your direct growth into their revenue growth — a mechanical alignment that survives personnel changes.
- **Attribution reporting:** monthly report of direct-site sessions, where-to-buy clicks, and modeled retail sales attributed to your owned media, by partner.

**(g) No downside case. This is the largest omission.** The prompt's central fact is that these partners *"have punished suppliers"* and that 55% of revenue sits with two accounts. The plan contains no war-game: what happens if a partner refuses the Charter, demands subscription be killed as a condition of the next line review, quietly reduces facings, cuts promotional support, or accelerates private label? There is no quantified exposure model (revenue/EBITDA impact of a 20% facing loss at Partner A), no trigger points, no kill switch, no BATNA, and no sequencing decision about *which* major to approach first and how to prevent them comparing notes. "Selective new physical (specialty, club, international, B2B/gift)" is one table row where a concentration-reduction roadmap with targets and timing should be.

**(h) No operating model or incentive design.** Who owns the direct P&L? How is a conflict between the sales VP and the DTC GM arbitrated, and by whom, on what timeline? Critically: a field sales organization compensated on retail sell-in will actively undermine DTC, and a DTC team on revenue targets will push discounts. Comp and internal transfer-pricing/credit rules are the real enforcement mechanism for everything in §4, and they are absent.

**(i) No investment case.** No capex/opex envelope, tech stack cost, headcount plan, fulfillment/3PL and returns economics, break-even timing, or funding source. The illustrative SKU math in §4 is useful but is not a channel P&L. An executive team cannot approve this document as written.

**(j) No demand-generation plan.** Having banned conquesting, retargeting off retailer properties, price leadership, and Q4 promotion, the plan never explains how traffic arrives. Owned/earned/creator strategy, SEO architecture, CRM lifecycle, subscription acquisition funnel and CAC assumptions by cohort are all missing — yet CAC of $6–9 is quoted as if solved.

**(k) No scorecard or stage gates.** There is a cadence table but no KPI set with targets and thresholds, no board review rhythm, and — importantly — no *partner health* leading indicators (share of shelf, distribution points, JBP score, promo support levels) tracked alongside DTC growth so conflict is detected before the angry call, not after.

**(l) Fulfillment/service quality unaddressed.** A direct channel that ships slower than the retailer it sits beside erodes brand equity and gives the buyer an easy talking point.

**(m) Operational conflict in the calendar.** Blackouts across both majors' tentpoles plus holiday plus back-to-school effectively removes DTC's ability to sell gifting sets and limited drops — two of the Tier A pillars — in their only viable window. This tension is real and needs an explicit resolution (e.g., non-price mechanics only during blackouts).

**(n) First Look allocation is unworkable as drafted.** Both majors cannot simultaneously hold right of first refusal on the same item. Specify the allocation rule (alternating, category-based, or committed-volume auction) before a partner discovers you promised the same thing twice — which would recreate the original trust breach in a worse form.

## 4. Accuracy and craft nits

- **Vendor references are loose.** Bazaarvoice is primarily ratings/reviews syndication, not where-to-buy; the category leaders are PriceSpider, MikMak, Channel Advisor. "Swiftly-type" is unclear. Habu is now part of LiveRamp. These small imprecisions cost credibility with an informed reader.
- **"direct-channel search demand by DRIVE/geography"** — undefined jargon; either define or cut.
- **No executive summary.** A plan of this complexity needs a one-page front end: the ask, the investment, the decision required, the three risks, and the target metrics.

## 5. What is genuinely strong (keep)

The diagnostic in §1 (it failed because it was a *store* and it was *discovered*) is sharp and correct. The "three commitments and one ask" gives the plan a spine. The insight that the buyer's anger was self-protective and that written commitments are internal ammunition is the most valuable sentence in the document. Decoupling identity capture from direct transactions (§5, Layer 1) is the right strategic call and is the part of the plan that actually delivers on the brief's data objective. Language discipline (§6.4), the pre-agreed concession menu, and reciprocal retail exclusivity (Tier D) are all high-quality, practitioner-grade moves. The tone — realistic about margin arriving on the second order, not the first — is right.

## 6. Priority fix list

1. Finish §6.6 and resolve the unilateral-policy-vs-signed-charter contradiction with counsel.
2. Add a downside/retaliation war-game with quantified exposure, triggers, and a concentration-reduction roadmap.
3. Rebuild the revenue target from a bottoms-up funnel; lower it if it doesn't hold.
4. Add operating model, incentive/comp design, and internal arbitration mechanism.
5. Add investment case and channel P&L with break-even.
6. Add unit-price guardrail with explicit math; drop the "different UPC solves it" framing.
7. Add demand-generation plan and CAC build.
8. Add KPI scorecard including partner-health leading indicators.
9. Resolve First Look allocation between the two majors; decide approach sequencing.
10. Check marketplace ToS exposure on connected packaging.

# Go-to-Market Plan: Building a Direct-to-Consumer Business Without Losing the Base

---

## 0. Executive Summary (one page)

**The decision requested.** Approve a three-year, $22M cumulative investment to build a direct channel architected as a *brand experience, data, and innovation asset* rather than a discount store — and approve the partner-facing sequence, beginning with a CEO-level top-to-top at both major accounts within 45 days.

**Why the first attempt failed.** The pilot was designed as a *store*, and it was *discovered*. A supplier site selling the same items at competitive prices is, from a buyer's chair, a competitor with better margins and no shelf rent. Discovery converted an economic disagreement into a trust breach, which is far harder to repair than a pricing dispute.

**The reframe.** Direct is a demand-generation, identity-capture and innovation-validation asset whose commercial output happens to include revenue. Every decision is tested against one question: *does this make the retailer's business with us better, worse, or neutral — and can we prove it with numbers they accept as theirs, not ours?*

**Illustrative baseline used throughout** (replace with actuals before board submission):

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Company net revenue | $500M |
| Gross margin (net of trade) | 42% ($210M) |
| Partner A | 32% of revenue ($160M); ~$60M GP; ~$30M EBITDA contribution |
| Partner B | 23% of revenue ($115M); ~$42M GP; ~$21M EBITDA contribution |
| Units sold annually | ~45M |
| Households buying the brand annually | ~18M (category: ~60M) |
| Current direct revenue | <$1M (paused pilot) |

**Targets — bottoms-up, deliberately conservative** (build shown in §3):

| Metric | Y1 | Y2 | Y3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct revenue | $2.7M | $9.6M | $22.4M |
| Direct as % of company revenue | 0.5% | 1.8% | **4.2%** (range 3–6%) |
| Consented identified profiles (cumulative) | 0.9M | 2.3M | **4.0M** |
| = % of annual brand-buying households | 5% | 13% | **22%** |
| Where-to-buy click-outs to partners | 1.1M | 3.2M | 6.5M |
| Direct contribution margin | −$5.9M | −$3.4M | +$1.1M |

We are explicitly **not** promising 8–12% of revenue direct. With price advantage removed, hero SKUs out of the cart, conquesting banned and peak weeks blacked out, 3–6% is the honest number. An inflated target is the single most likely cause of the discounting that would blow up the retail relationships.

**The three risks, named up front.**
1. **Retaliation.** A 20% facing reduction at Partner A costs ~$5–7M gross profit — more than three years of direct contribution. Mitigation: §8 war-game, early-warning triggers, pre-authorized pause states.
2. **Legal exposure.** Bilateral price commitments to two dominant customers create a hub-and-spoke fact pattern with a signed document as evidence. Mitigation: §9 — pricing policy is *unilateral and publicly announced*, never negotiated, and is absent from the partner charter.
3. **Internal sabotage.** A field organization paid on retail sell-in will kill this quietly. Mitigation: §6 comp and credit design.

---

## 1. Strategic Frame: Three Principles and One Ask

The substance of the original "three commitments" is right; the *mechanism* has changed for legal reasons (§9).

**Announced publicly to the market — not negotiated with any customer:**

- **Principle 1 — Price position.** Our owned channel is positioned as the price ceiling for our brand, not the floor. We set direct prices unilaterally under a published *Brand Pricing Principles* statement addressed to consumers, all trade customers and the press simultaneously. It is a statement of what we do, not a promise to any customer, and it is not open to discussion, modification or bilateral confirmation.
- **Principle 2 — Assortment.** Core, high-velocity items are never direct-exclusive. New items go to retail on a published First Look calendar (§4, Tier B) with a mechanical, disclosed allocation rule.
- **Principle 3 — Reinvestment.** A defined *absolute dollar floor* of retail media, shopper marketing and validated innovation flows back into partner businesses, committed inside Joint Business Planning and auditable via the retailer's own media invoices (§5.4).

**The ask, made bilaterally and legitimately:** collaborative measurement and data access — clean-room participation, loyalty-matched incrementality testing, and joint credit for demand our owned media creates.

---

## 2. Channel Architecture

| Channel | Primary job | Assortment | Price position |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Brand Home** (owned site) | Education, discovery, identity capture, where-to-buy | Full catalog **visible**; differentiated set **buyable** | MSRP reference; never a price leader |
| **Direct Commerce** (inside Brand Home) | Subscription, personalization, systems, long tail, refurb | Tier A + Tier C only (§4) | Governed by the unit-price guardrail (§5.1) |
| **National retail incl. Partners A & B** | Volume, penetration, trial, physical availability | Core heroes, retailer-exclusive packs, seasonal | Retailer's sole discretion |
| **Retailer .com / marketplaces (1P & 3P)** | Digital shelf, search capture, review volume | Core + retailer-specific packs | Retailer's discretion; we fund content/media |
| **Diversification portfolio** (third national, club, specialty, international, B2B/gift/corporate) | Structural concentration reduction (§8.4) | Channel-appropriate packs | Channel norm |

### 2.1 Where-to-Buy is a first-class feature

Every product page carries live retailer availability and price via a where-to-buy provider — **PriceSpider, MikMak or Channel Advisor** are the category leaders (note: Bazaarvoice is ratings/reviews syndication, a separate need, not where-to-buy). Both majors appear above the direct cart on comparable items.

**Measurement must be theirs, not ours.** We will *not* present supplier-modelled "attributed retail sales"; sophisticated buyers discount and resent it. Instead:

- We report only what is objectively verifiable and unarguable: sessions, product-page views by item, where-to-buy click-outs to each partner, and search-demand signal by market.
- **Incrementality is measured inside the retailer's own environment** — Walmart Luminate / Walmart Connect, Roundel and 84.51° (Kroger), Amazon Marketing Cloud, Instacart Ads — using our consented audiences matched in a clean room. The retailer's analytics team owns the readout. We agree the test design and success criteria in advance, in writing, and we accept the result even if unflattering.
- Year-one commitment: two jointly designed incrementality tests per major partner. Nothing about the value of Brand Home traffic is asserted before those tests read out.

### 2.2 Buyable ≠ visible

The full catalog is browsable — SEO, education, reviews, comparison, troubleshooting — while only the differentiated set is in the cart. We own the search result without owning the transaction. Every non-buyable page's primary CTA is where-to-buy; the secondary CTA is identity capture (§7).
